title: WHAT SERVICE COULD I SELL?
content:
People often dismiss their most sellable skills because those skills feel ordinary to them.

Look beyond formal qualifications. Think about tasks you perform at work, hobbies you've practiced for years, software you know well, equipment you can use, practical problems you solve, things friends ask you to help with, and knowledge you barely notice anymore because it has become easy for you.

Customers do not only pay for rare genius. They pay to save time, avoid frustration, borrow expertise, get something done correctly, or receive a result they cannot or do not want to produce themselves.

START WITH EVIDENCE FROM YOUR OWN LIFE
Look at what employers trust you to do, tasks you perform quickly, problems friends bring you, hobbies where you have accumulated skill or equipment, and things you have organized, repaired, written, taught, planned, cleaned, built, researched, or managed.

CONNECT THE SKILL TO A CUSTOMER
"Good with spreadsheets" is a skill. "Create simple inventory trackers for small craft businesses" begins to resemble a service. "Good at organizing" is a skill. "Help busy families unpack and organize after a move" is closer to something someone can buy.

You do not have to force the answer alone. The next guide can interview you and look for those connections.

SKILL-TO-SERVICE EXAMPLES
Work skill: You schedule complex jobs -> scheduling/coordination support for a specific kind of small business.
Hobby skill: You restore furniture -> furniture restoration or refinishing.
Practical skill: You are unusually good at packing and organizing moves -> packing/unpacking service.
Technical skill: You build reliable spreadsheets -> spreadsheet setup or cleanup for a particular customer type.

These examples are not a menu to choose from. They demonstrate the move from "something I know how to do" to "a result someone could pay for."

I ALREADY HAVE A SERVICE IDEA → PDF 42.
I NEED HELP FIGURING OUT WHAT I COULD OFFER → PDF 41.

YOU DO NOT NEED TO BE THE WORLD'S BEST
A service does not require you to be the top expert in a field. It does require you to be able to perform the promised work competently and honestly.

The useful comparison is not "Am I better than every professional doing this?" It is "Can I reliably create a result that this customer would reasonably pay for, and am I qualified to provide it?"

LOOK FOR EVIDENCE INSTEAD OF TRYING TO INVENT A TALENT

Start with your actual life.

What have you been paid to do at work, even if it was not your job title? What do coworkers rely on you for? What do friends or relatives ask you to help with? What have you learned through hobbies, parenting, home ownership, volunteering, caregiving, side projects, or solving your own problems?

Then look for capabilities underneath the activity.

"Worked in an office" is vague. Scheduling, spreadsheet cleanup, customer communication, invoice tracking, document organization, data entry, and process documentation are sellable capabilities.

"I like dogs" is an interest. Dog walking, pet sitting, basic grooming, pet photography, training support within your qualifications, or creating organized pet-care routines are possible services.

"I am good with computers" becomes more useful when translated into specific work such as device setup, software onboarding, spreadsheet building, website updates, or technical support within your actual competence.

The point is not to turn every ability into a business. It is to produce a short list of services grounded in evidence about what you can genuinely do.

FROM EXPERIENCE TO A POSSIBLE SERVICE

Suppose you worked for years in a warehouse and think, "I don't have a sellable professional skill."

That conclusion may be wrong, but the solution is not to flatter yourself into claiming expertise you do not have.

Break the work down. Perhaps you trained new employees, maintained inventory spreadsheets, scheduled work, troubleshot scanners, documented procedures, organized storage, communicated with carriers, or became unusually good at finding discrepancies.

Some of those abilities may transfer into services. Inventory spreadsheet cleanup for a small business is more concrete than "operations consulting." Writing simple standard operating procedures is more concrete than "business optimization."

Now check competence. Could you reliably produce the promised result for a paying customer? What would be outside your knowledge? Does the work require a license, certification, insurance, or other qualification? What would you need to learn or verify?

The goal is to find the overlap between something useful and something you can responsibly deliver.

WHAT THIS GUIDE SHOULD PRODUCE

You should leave with a short list of service possibilities supported by actual evidence from your life.

For each possibility, you should be able to point to something concrete:

"I have done this repeatedly."

"People already ask me for help with this."

"I know this process well."

"I have equipment that lets me do this."

"I can produce this result competently."

"I understand this customer or environment."

Then ask what you would still need to learn before charging.

That last question matters. Recognizing a sellable ability does not mean overstating your qualifications. The goal is to find the intersection between something useful you can responsibly deliver and a problem another person may pay to solve.

IF YOU HAVE TOO MANY POSSIBLE SERVICES

Do not pick the one that sounds most impressive.

Compare them using four practical filters:

Can I responsibly deliver the result now, or with a realistic amount of additional preparation?

Do I actually want to perform this work repeatedly?

Does it fit my available time, location, equipment, and other constraints?

Can I describe a plausible person or business that has this problem?

A service that scores well on those questions is worth exploring even if it sounds ordinary.

Ordinary useful work is sellable work.

WHERE TO GO NEXT
If you already see a service you could sell, continue to PDF 42. If you need help discovering possibilities from your actual background, use PDF 41 first.
